evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

package.documentation:
This simulator is built from Johnson, Aylward & Stricker (Health Policy, 2011), a 2009-2010 web survey of 2424 U.S. residents with clinically diagnosed, laboratory-supported chronic Lyme disease (symptoms ≥6 months despite ≥21 days of antibiotics), recruited through a Lyme disease patient-advocacy organization (a non-random, self-selected sample).

Inputs model findings from Table 2 and Figure 2: (1-2) the size and 10+-physician count for the CDC two-tier/Western-blot-positive subgroup (n=1000); (3-4) the same for the other-supporting-lab-test subgroup (n=1424); the two count inputs' ranges were narrowed around the document's own reported values specifically so the comparison direction cannot be reversed by slider movement, preserving the document's reported statistically significant difference (p=0.0001); (5) the percentage of post-diagnosis insurance applicants (n=416) denied coverage; (6) the percentage of disability applicants (n=739) denied specifically for not conforming to one professional society's (IDSA's) Lyme treatment guidelines.

Outputs recompute each subgroup's 10+-physician rate, their percentage-point gap, the insurance-denial rate, and the guideline-linked disability-denial rate, directly from the inputs above.

**Limitations.** This survey collected no dollar-denominated cost, income-loss, or caregiving-time data; every output here is a utilization or access percentage, not a cost figure. All pooled percentages in this document - including every output modeled here - have not been checked for variation by age, sex/gender, race/ethnicity, or disability status; the authors state these variables were not assessed in their survey. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports disaggregated analysis of this kind even though this document did not perform one.

Separately, this document describes a systemic evidence/care-system limitation: IDSA's Lyme treatment guidelines are described as shaping hospital antibiotic-treatment protocols and physician hospital privileges, and are cited directly by disability insurers as grounds for benefit denial, with no counterbalancing formal guideline-pluralism mechanism described as being in place at the time of the study.

This survey's self-selected, chronic/lab-confirmed respondent population should not be pooled with CDC national surveillance case counts, external cost-of-illness studies (e.g., Zhang et al. 2006), or older surveys (e.g., Vanderhoof 1993) cited elsewhere in the document; those describe different populations and are not used as inputs here.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- CDC-reported new Lyme disease cases in the United States (2008, the United States): the document reports 35,198; CDC's reported cases were 35,198 (confirmed and probable together), so the document's figure is within 10% of the CDC confirmed-plus-probable total (+0.0% versus the total). Definitions may differ between the document and CDC surveillance, so a gap is a prompt to check, not an error. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- CDC-cited low-end estimate of true annual Lyme disease cases (6x reported) (2008, the United States): the document's estimate of 200,000 is 5.7 times the 35,198 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- CDC-cited high-end estimate of true annual Lyme disease cases (12x reported) (2008, the United States): the document's estimate of 400,000 is 11.4 times the 35,198 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right.
